blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Leading through conflict in a British team is less about resolving the immediate flare-up and more about setting an ongoing tone where conflict becomes usable rather than destructive. The best British leaders do not avoid conflict — they make it safe. They acknowledge that disagreement is part of doing serious work, and they show, by example, that a disagreement handled calmly rarely damages the relationship it passes through.

The practical discipline has three parts. First, name the disagreement quickly, without drama. Second, separate the work from the people: two colleagues who disagree on a decision are not, by definition, at war with each other. Third, give both sides a chance to step back gracefully if new information changes their view — without making either one feel they have lost anything by moving.

Done well over years, this quietly shapes a British team into one of the most productive forms of group that exists: calm on the surface, honest underneath, capable of debating hard without breaking. And that, more than any strategy, is what lets senior British teams outlast harder-charging competitors over long cycles.

items.q: According to the text, what is leading through conflict in a British team mainly about?
options: Resolving the immediate flare-up as fast as possible
Winning each individual argument decisively
Setting an ongoing tone where conflict becomes usable
Avoiding disagreement so relationships stay intact
items.why: "less about resolving the immediate flare-up and more about setting an ongoing tone where conflict becomes usable".

items.q: What is the SECOND part of the practical discipline described?
options: Let both sides step back gracefully
Name the disagreement quickly, without drama
Separate the work from the people
Escalate the issue to a senior sponsor
items.why: "Second, separate the work from the people."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Letting someone change their mind should carry no penalty.
Disagreement is a normal part of serious work.
Handled calmly, disagreement rarely harms a relationship.
A leader who suppresses conflict is protecting the team.
items.why: Inferência: o texto defende tornar o conflito seguro, não suprimi-lo — suprimir contraria toda a tese.

items.q: The phrase "calm on the surface, honest underneath" most strongly suggests that…
options: British teams hide their real opinions to keep the peace
outward composure and candid debate can coexist
honesty is only possible once tempers have cooled
surface calm is a sign that no real work is happening
items.why: Inferência: a calma externa não impede o debate franco — os dois convivem, e é isso que torna o grupo produtivo.

items.q: Why, according to the text, can such teams outlast harder-charging competitors?
options: They avoid the disagreements that slow rivals down
They debate hard without breaking, over long cycles
They spend less on strategy than their rivals do
They replace their leadership more frequently
items.why: "capable of debating hard without breaking… is what lets senior British teams outlast harder-charging competitors over long cycles."

blocks.instruction: Ouça Sophie orientando um diretor sênior. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
So, before we go any further, let me reflect back what I'm hearing. Your team hasn't become more harmonious — it's gone quiet. And those are very different things.

When people stop disagreeing with you, the usual reading is that they've come round to your view. In my experience it's almost never that. What's happened is that the cost of speaking up has crept above the cost of staying silent, and your best people have quietly done the maths.

Now, I wouldn't rush to fix this with a big speech about candour — that tends to make it worse. Instead, I'd start much smaller. Next time someone raises even a mild objection, resist the urge to close it down. Sit with it. Ask a genuine question. And whatever you do, don't win too quickly.

Might it be worth naming the pattern out loud, gently? Something like, "I wonder whether we've stopped challenging each other." You're not accusing anyone — you're giving them permission. In a British team, that permission usually has to come from the top, and it has to come more than once before anyone believes it.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: How does Sophie characterise the change in the director's team?
options: It has gone quiet, which is not the same as harmonious
It has grown openly hostile toward the director
It has become genuinely more harmonious
It has split into two competing factions
items.why: "Your team hasn't become more harmonious — it's gone quiet. And those are very different things."

items.q: According to Sophie, what has actually happened when people stop disagreeing?
options: They have lost interest in the work entirely
The team has run out of things to disagree about
They have genuinely been persuaded by the director
The cost of speaking up has risen above the cost of staying silent
items.why: "the cost of speaking up has crept above the cost of staying silent, and your best people have quietly done the maths."

items.q: Why does Sophie warn against "a big speech about candour"?
options: The team has already heard that speech before
The director is not a confident public speaker
There is not enough time before the next meeting
It tends to make the problem worse rather than better
items.why: "I wouldn't rush to fix this with a big speech about candour — that tends to make it worse."

items.q: When Sophie says "don't win too quickly," she is implying that…
options: the director should let others reach the decision first
the director tends to lose most arguments anyway
shutting objections down fast is what silenced the team
quick decisions are always worse than slow ones
items.why: Inferência: fechar objeções rápido demais ensina as pessoas a se calarem — daí o silêncio atual.

items.q: What does Sophie suggest about giving 'permission' to challenge in a British team?
options: It only works if it is put in writing
It must come from the top, and be repeated before anyone believes it
It should be granted once and then left alone
It is best delegated to a neutral facilitator
items.why: "that permission usually has to come from the top, and it has to come more than once before anyone believes it."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "She defused the flare-up before it spread to the wider team." A flare-up is…
options: a formal written complaint
a sudden, sharp outburst of conflict
a long-running strategic dispute
a scheduled performance review
items.why: Flare-up = explosão / estopim: um conflito que irrompe de repente.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Handled well, friction between two directors is ___ — it sharpens the decision."
options: hard-charging
destructive
usable
at war
items.why: Usable = útil: o atrito vira algo aproveitável em vez de danoso.

items.q: "Two people who disagree on a forecast are not, by definition, at war." To be at war here means to be…
options: working on different projects
competing for the same promotion
aligned on the outcome
in open, personal hostility
items.why: At war = em guerra: hostilidade pessoal aberta, que a lição diz não ser consequência automática de discordar.

items.q: "A calm British team can quietly outlast flashier rivals." To outlast means to…
options: grow faster than
openly outperform in the short term
imitate the tactics of
endure longer than
items.why: To outlast = resistir mais: durar mais que o outro ao longo do tempo.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "When the data shifted, he let her ___ from her position without any loss of face."
options: roll out
outlast
step back
flare up
items.why: To step back = recuar: rever a posição sem sentir que perdeu algo.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem quando se lidera equipes em conflito. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Rather than shut it down, she chose to sit with the objection for a moment." To sit with something means to…
options: dismiss it politely
put it in writing
let it stay and consider it properly
delegate it to someone else
items.why: Sit with = deixar a questão respirar e refletir sobre ela em vez de cortá-la de imediato.

items.q: "The moment tempers rose, the chair stepped in to talk them down." To talk someone down means to…
options: exclude them from the meeting
criticise them in public
overrule their decision
persuade them to be calmer
items.why: Talk down = acalmar alguém pela conversa, baixar a temperatura.

items.q: "Two managers pushed back on the timeline in the review." They…
options: approved it without comment
rewrote it overnight
forgot to read it
resisted or challenged it
items.why: Push back on = resistir, contestar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "Let's not paper over the disagreement just to end the meeting on time." To paper over means to…
options: solve it permanently
document it formally
hide a problem instead of resolving it
escalate it to the board
items.why: Paper over (the cracks) = disfarçar o problema por cima, sem resolver de fato.

items.q: "Once it's settled, this team is expected to move on without holding grudges." To move on means to…
options: leave the matter behind and carry forward
transfer to another department
escalate to HR
reopen the argument later
items.why: Move on = seguir em frente depois de resolver, sem carregar ressentimento — exatamente o que a cultura britânica espera.
